title: MIRA: Reinforcing Multimodal Reasoning via Deceptive Contextual Augmentation
claim: A two-stage procedure first builds filtered misleading-context training data, then uses it in an RL loop with group-level triggers.
layout: 2 stacked dashed panels, left-to-right flow, numbered stages with feedback loop
description: The figure has two stacked dashed-border sections. The top section, "Construction of Pseudo Visual Error Data", has four pastel boxes joined by arrows. First is the input: a school schedule table image and a question. Second is correct context generation by a policy model, with a green correct description. Third is corrupted context modification by an expert model (OpenAI logo), with a red corrupted description and a modification record. Fourth is data filtering by the policy model, with judge checks marked correct or incorrect, a save icon for retained samples and a trash icon for discarded ones. The bottom section, "RL Training of MIRA Method", flows left to right. It starts from an error visual context input in red, adds intra-group triggers (trigger / no trigger), then trajectory sampling by the policy model, rollouts y0..yn, and an RL process box with the reward and group-advantage equations and a policy gradient update. A feedback arrow labeled Update returns to the policy model.
caption: Overview of MIRA. MIRA consists of two parts. The top illustrates the construction of deceptive visual context using the policy model and an expert model. The bottom shows the training process; compared to GRPO, the key changes are modified inputs and the use of intra-group triggers.
abstract: While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has significantly advanced multimodal reasoning, existing frameworks suffer from a critical "perception-reasoning gap." Due to an over-reliance on seemingly relevant visual tokens, even minor perceptual perturbations can propagate through the reasoning process, leading to compounding hallucinations. To address this issue, we propose MIRA, a training framework that improves robustness to erroneous visual contexts while enhancing logical reasoning ability. By injecting filtered, deceptive visual contexts during training, we construct challenging "hard traps" that stress-test the model's robustness to misleading information. Furthermore, we introduce a group-wise reflection-triggering mechanism that enables the model to autonomously detect and rectify inconsistencies between visual cues and logical constraints, which is ultimately internalized as an intrinsic policy behavior. Importantly, MIRA does not rely on human annotations. Experimental results across multiple reasoning and perception benchmarks show that MIRA yields an average 7% improvement on in-domain benchmarks, with consistent improvements on vision-centric benchmarks. These findings highlight that active error recovery is essential for robust multimodal reasoning. Comprehensive ablation studies and analyses further provide insights into why MIRA is effective.
